[0] Apple and other tech giants may have to pay the EU an annual fixed sum under a revised version of a digital services tax plan.

[1] The EU hopes that by modifying its earlier proposal, it can increase tax revenue while avoiding provoking the wrath of the White House…

[2] EU member states have long been divided over the digital services tax. Examples under Apple include iCloud, Apple Music, Apple TV, and Apple Creator Studio, among others.

[3] Critics note that companies earn substantial revenue from selling subscription services to EU citizens, yet may not pay tax in Europe on those earnings. Others worry the tax would disproportionately hit European firms, and some fear taxing American companies would invite retaliation from the White House.

[4] The Financial Times reports that the European Commission has now put forward a compromise intended to satisfy all sides — except, of course, the companies such as Apple, Google, and Meta that would have to pay the new levy.

[5] Officials say Brussels is considering revising an existing proposal to require all companies operating in the EU with annual revenues above €100 million to pay a fixed annual amount… Officials believe that by adjusting the thresholds and the levy in the Core proposal to cover only very large companies, it can both increase the sums collected from tech groups and address European criticism that Core would hit many mid-sized European companies.

[6] The revised plan would not single out companies that sell digital services, but would apply to all large companies. Since it was the earlier proposal that led the White House to threaten retaliatory tariffs, the EU hopes the new version will not trigger another trade fight with the United States.

[7] Top comment posted by cubbuc

[8] I have no problem taxing large tech companies. But we have to be clear at this point: we must admit that the companies capable of growing to that scale simply do not get born in Europe, and if they do, our limp-wristed regulators cannot prevent them from being acquired by American giants.

[9] You can keep playing this pointless cat-and-mouse game with American tech companies. You will lose.

[10] Or you can actually start doing the hard work of fixing what is clearly a structural and systemic problem on this continent.

[11] The exact levy per company has not yet been set. The plan is to first reach agreement on the principle among the EU's 27 member states, and then set the rate.

[12] 9to5Mac's view

[13] This mess was supposed to be resolved by a global deal brokered by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). That deal would have ensured that companies around the world paid at least some tax in each of the countries where they operate, and Apple supported it.

[14] However, Donald Trump pulled the United States out of that deal, prompting calls for the EU to produce its own version. Saying Trump would not object to this revised approach strikes me as optimistic.
